items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: Actually, J.J. Johnson joined the band in 1942, in September, when we were on the way to California, we picked up J.J. Johnson in Indianapolis.

ctx.x: Right. Now in these groups that you led in '43, '44 -- this was a time I think, when you began to pick up a number of younger musicians. For a long time, you know, in your bands, you would have people you could always count on -- came in and out. But now a new generation was arising during, and just after World War II, and you began to pick up some musicians who were much younger. Among them, I think -- well, you tell me.
Well, you probably have in mind J.J. Johnson and Max Ranch Rose -- people like that.

items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: J. J. Johnson joined me in Indianapolis [Indiana] and came to California with me... J. J. Johnson went on to become a very talented arranger, and he contributed some charts to your band early on. Yes, he did.

ctx.x: You just mentioned that a lot of people were getting drafted. Was that the only reason these people came in, or did you want to inject a different kind of sound or you were attracted to some of these younger musicians?

No, but, I mean, some of those I replaced because they went into the service. But, no, I don’t know. Just, you know, J. J. Johnson joined me in Indianapolis [Indiana] and came to California with me. Now, when Max Roach came into the band, I don’t remember. Miles Davis was in the band in ’46, something, and he was with it for just a short time, maybe a matter of weeks.
You picked him up in St. Louis [Missouri], is that correct?

items.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I was with Benny Carter for about two or three years.

ctx.x: Yeah, I think it was Clarence Love. I think it was LaVon Kemp, I think Clarence Love was the next situation, and then Snookum Russell. The Snookum Russell thing was important. It was a very good band. They traveled a lot. It was in the Snookum Russell band that I met Fats Navarro, who was certainly to become one of the giants of jazz in later years. Fats Navarro and I were road buddies. We rode side by side. We’d sit side by side on the bus. We roomed together. We were true buddy- buddy buddies. Fats was a big…
situation was Benny Carter, I believe.

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: JJ. Johnson has ... actually, JJ. Johnson is now doing "The Six Million Dollar Man" which, you know ... he has taken over on that.

ctx.x: JJ. Johnson has ... actually, JJ. Johnson is now doing "The Six Million Dollar Man" which, you know ... he has taken over on that. After Oliver Nelson passed away. Last year. And Benny Golson, we must remember, too.

And you saw all these people coming in? I mean, they came in while you were there. Did they -- did their work begin with one film, usually -- how did they break in? I mean, what was the process? Did they come there for one particular purpose -- with a contract already in their hands, or did they just come there and say, well, "Here I am. I'm gonna try to get some work in the studios."?
